headline: In Arizona, Hobbs and Democrats outspent Turning Point's $18 million Biggs bet
dek: Gov. Katie Hobbs and a county Democratic committee funded by the Democratic Governors Association spent far more than Andy Biggs. That gap held even after Turning Point put more than $18 million behind Biggs. Hobbs won by 13 points.
summary: Hobbs, her campaign and Democratic party money outspent Biggs and Turning Point by a wide margin; she won by 13 points.

paras.text: Arizona's race on The Watch's wave this year was not a federal one, so there are no FEC numbers to follow. The money in the governor's race moved through state committees. Tracking it means reading the state's own filings and the local reporting on them.

The short version: Gov. Katie Hobbs, a Democrat, and the committees behind her spent far more than U.S. Rep. Andy Biggs, the Republican nominee. Hobbs won 1,414,266 votes to 1,080,353, a 13.1-point margin, in a state Donald Trump carried by 5.5 points in 2024. The Associated Press called the race Wednesday morning.

The Oct. 15 reports were the last before Election Day. In them, Hobbs' campaign had spent more than $17 million on the race, and Biggs just over $5 million. The candidates' own reports tell only part of the story.

Hobbs's side spread its money across several accounts. The biggest was a county party. The Arizona Daily Star described the Navajo County Democratic Committee as being used to funnel both donations and expenses, not just for Hobbs but other Democratic candidates. It reported more than $33.2 million in expenses, including more than $21 million on broadcast advertising. State law does not require political parties to break down how much of that was spent on behalf of Hobbs.

Much of that money came from the Democratic Governors Association. According to the filings described by the Star, the association's Arizona committee collected more than $17.3 million from corporations and limited liability companies and transferred $16.9 million of that to the Navajo County Democratic Committee. Copper State Values, a PAC allied with Hobbs, transferred $6 million to the county committee as well. The association announced its first $10 million in July. By late October it had spent $14 million on the race. The Republican Governors Association had not spent any money.

The Biggs side was simpler. Biggs ran a single committee, and most of the help came from Turning Point, the Phoenix-based conservative group founded by the late Charlie Kirk. The Arizona Capitol Times reported that Biggs was being bolstered by $18.3 million from Turning Point Action, the group's political-spending arm. Other reports credit that spending to its state committee, Turning Point PAC. In the Star's breakdown, $5.9 million went to pro-Biggs advertising and $12.8 million from outside groups went to convincing people not to vote for Hobbs, $12.3 million of it from Turning Point.

The donors behind Turning Point are only partly public. Arizona's 2022 Voters' Right to Know Act, its "dark money" law, requires groups spending at least $50,000 in campaigns to disclose individual contributors giving more than $5,000. In the spring a Democratic student PAC filed a complaint alleging that Turning Point's two political arms had not filed those reports. By the end of the race, the Star cited dark-money disclosures showing Turning Point's PAC had spent over $18 million since June.

Reports also disagree about a smaller Republican committee, Republican Leadership for Arizona. One Star account called it an arm of the Arizona Republican Party that put in $2.1 million. A later one said it was largely funded by the conservative Club For Growth and spent over $3.8 million to help Biggs.

Hobbs went on the air early. Her first ads, on television, radio and online, highlighted her working-class background, including stints in fast food, driving for Uber, and working as a social worker. By September her campaign said it had spent over $14 million on TV and streaming since late May. Two Arizona media buyers estimated she had outspent Biggs at least 15-to-1 on advertising. Biggs's first summer attack ad went straight to social media, a far cheaper route than a broadcast buy.

The ads turned to attacks. Hobbs ran four ads branding Biggs a "predator protector." Most dealt with his role as Senate president in 2013 in the death of a bill to dissolve the police department in the polygamous community of Colorado City. The Star noted that strictly speaking, he didn't kill the bill. Biggs answered with an ad accusing Hobbs of vetoing four bills aimed at "predators and pornographers." Another Biggs ad said she was under criminal investigation over Sunshine Residential Homes, a state contractor whose owners had given to her political operation. In August the attorney general's criminal division chief reported that agents had found no evidence to substantiate a pay-for-play scheme.

Turning Point's money also bought less visible work. It paid for roadside signs in English and Spanish reading "Democrats for Biggs." The Arizona Republic could find no evidence that any organized coalition of Democrats backing Biggs existed. Its text-message campaigns were produced by contractors 1Ten and Engaged America LLC, both owned by state Sen. Jake Hoffman. Hoffman opened a Senate inquiry into Hobbs while his consulting business had received more than $1.2 million to help Biggs unseat her. Senate Republicans later put former Arizona Supreme Court Justice Andrew Gould in charge of the inquiry.
Did the money buy the seat?

The side that spent more won, and won by a lot. Hobbs led Biggs in eight October polls. Her 13.1-point margin is an 18.7-point swing from the 2024 presidential vote. She is the first Democrat to win reelection as Arizona governor since Janet Napolitano in 2006.

Turning Point's spending narrowed the money gap but not the vote. The Deseret News found Biggs lost the East Valley, the suburbs around his own congressional district, by 10.6 percentage points, a 21-point shift from 2024. Money was not the only explanation people offered. A Biggs relative who won a state House seat told the Deseret News that the national narrative mattered more than the particulars. Others pointed to Hobbs's choice of former Mesa Mayor John Giles, a former Republican, as her running mate. The Capitol Times reported that Turning Point's candidates struggled in the general election, contributing to a likely Democratic sweep of statewide offices for the first time in decades. The national Republican governors' group never spent in the race. Readers can weigh whether the money, the candidates or the year made the difference.
